In preview search when an early appearing set was presented in a 3D surface, observers subsequently had difficulty detecting new targets that occurred in the same surface, and this was true even if the new surface was defined by the same items as the old surface, and even if the old items were not present in the final display.

In summary, our research is concerned with
how observers use information from a preview display to guide their search for targets in a subsequent test display.
the role of inhibition in search and how it is influenced by the properties of the stimuli.
the mechanisms underlying the selection of objects and surfaces in visual search.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the carry-over effect in search is a function of the surface properties of the items, and that these properties are encoded by the observer in the first few seconds of a trial, and that this information can be used to inhibit the detection of items that share the surface properties of those that have just been ignored.
the results of this study are consistent with the hypothesis that inhibitory processes are not restricted to simple feature based items, but can be directed to more complex objects such as surfaces.
the carry-over effect is due to a surface-based inhibition process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the negative carry-over effect can be extended to the case of surfaces and is mediated by binocular depth cues.
preview search involves a combination of inhibition of distractors and their surface features and facilitation of targets.
previewed distractors and the features they share with targets may be inhibited in visual search, even when the distractors are defined by 3-D surfaces.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the negative carryover effect is not a feature based process, but a process based on the formation of surface representations.
the negative carryover effects can occur in the absence of common features between old and new distractors, and that the carryover effects can be obtained with a surface-based display.
inhibition can be directed towards a surface defined by the spatial configuration of items in the absence of any shared feature.
